questions.prompt: How many bytes does the string `"Hola"` occupy in memory?
questions.explain: A C string ends with the null character `'\0'`: a string of length n needs n + 1 bytes.
options: It depends on the length of the program
option_notes: A literal has a fixed size.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: `strlen` counts the characters before the `'\0'` (4) while `sizeof` of the array includes the terminator (5).

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (The terminator ends the string.)
questions.explain: Writing a `'\0'` into the middle shortens the string: functions stop at the first one.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: `a == b` compares the ADDRESSES of the two arrays (different, so 0). `strcmp` compares the contents and returns 0 when they are equal.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: `strcat` makes it `abcd`. Then `strcpy(buf + 1, "XY")` overwrites from index 1 and writes its own terminator, so the string becomes `aXY`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: `strchr` finds the FIRST `o` (index 4) and `strrchr` the LAST one (index 7). Subtracting the start gives the position.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `char s[] = "hi";` and `char *p = "hi";`?
questions.explain: The array holds its own copy that you may change. A pointer to a literal points to read-only memory: writing through it is undefined behaviour (usually a crash).
options: `s` is a modifiable copy of the text; `p` points to a string literal that must not be modified
`s` is on the heap and `p` on the stack
option_notes: They differ in whether you can modify the text.
It is the other way round.
The array is on the stack; the literal is in static read-only data.

questions.prompt: How do you correctly test whether two strings `a` and `b` have the same text?
questions.explain: `strcmp` returns 0 for equal strings (negative or positive otherwise). `==` compares addresses and `=` copies nothing.
option_notes: That is TRUE when the strings DIFFER.
That assigns a pointer (and does not compile for arrays).

questions.prompt: To store a copy of the string `s` on the heap, how many bytes must you allocate?
questions.explain: The copy needs room for every character plus the terminating `'\0'`. (`sizeof(s)` would be the size of the pointer if `s` is a `char *`.)
option_notes: One byte short: the terminator would overflow.
For a pointer that is 8, not the text length.
Wasteful and unrelated to the terminator.

questions.prompt: Which of these calls can write beyond the end of a destination buffer that is too small?
questions.explain: `strcpy` and `strcat` do not know the size of `dst`. `strlen` only reads. `strncpy` is bounded (but does not add a terminator if the source is long).
option_notes: Bounded by the count (check the terminator).

questions.prompt: `strcmp(a, b)` returns {{0}} when the two strings are equal.
questions.explain: A negative number means `a` comes before `b`, a positive number after; zero means equal.

questions.prompt: Complete the idiom that removes the trailing newline that `fgets` leaves in `line`.
questions.explain: `strcspn(line, "\n")` is the index of the first newline (or the length if there is none): writing `'\0'` there cuts the line.

questions.prompt: Match each string function with what it does.
questions.explain: These live in `<string.h>`. Remember that `strdup` allocates memory you must `free`.
pairs: counts the characters before the terminator
finds the first occurrence of a character
returns a malloc'ed copy of a string

questions.prompt: Sort these string functions by how they behave with respect to the destination size.
questions.explain: The unbounded functions are a source of buffer overflows; prefer the versions that take a size (`snprintf`, `strncat`, and `strncpy` with care).

questions.prompt: Which of these initialises a string correctly?
questions.explain: A brace list of characters initialises an ARRAY. `char *s = {...}` is not valid (a course slide shows it), `char s = "Hola"` stores a pointer in a char, and C has no `string` type.
option_notes: A pointer cannot be initialised with a list of chars.
A single char cannot hold a string.
There is no `string` type in C.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (strncmp compares only n characters.)
questions.explain: The first two characters `ap` are equal, so `strncmp` returns 0. `strstr` returns a pointer to the first occurrence of `tw`, so printing it shows `two`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: `strtok_r` returns the pieces between the delimiters, one per call, and skips empty fields (`a::b` has no piece between the two colons). Later calls pass `NULL`; the position is kept in `save`. It writes `'\0'` into the string, so it needs a modifiable array.

questions.prompt: What does `strncat(dst, src, n)` do?
questions.explain: The destination needs room for `strlen(dst) + n + 1` bytes. Unlike `strncpy`, `strncat` always terminates the result.
options: Appends at most n characters of src to dst and always adds the terminator
Appends exactly n characters even past the end of src
option_notes: It stops at the end of src.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: `toupper` converts a lower-case letter to upper case and `tolower` the opposite; other characters are unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which of these return non-zero for the character `'7'`?
questions.explain: `'7'` is a decimal digit, so it is also alphanumeric and a hexadecimal digit. It is not a letter and not punctuation.

questions.prompt: Sort these characters by the kind of character they are.
questions.explain: `isalpha`, `isdigit`, `isspace` and `ispunct` classify characters; the newline counts as white space.

questions.prompt: Match each character test with what it checks.
questions.explain: These tests come from `<ctype.h>`.
pairs: a printable character, including the space
a printable character except the space
a control character such as the newline

questions.prompt: Why do programs cast the argument of `isalpha` and similar functions to `unsigned char`?
questions.explain: Where `char` is signed, bytes above 127 become negative numbers, which these functions do not accept. Write `isalpha((unsigned char) c)`.
options: Their argument must be an unsigned char value or EOF; a negative char value is undefined behaviour
option_notes: The cast has no speed effect.
